slot.brief: Determine the intervals where a function involving e^x times a polynomial (or log-composite) is strictly increasing, solving a derivative-sign inequality; hardest variant with parameter.

stem: For which values of $a$ is $f(x)=e^x(x^2+ax+2)$ strictly increasing on $[-2,2]$?

verdicts.working: Let b=a+2. Then f'(x)=e^x(x^2+bx+b). Nonnegativity on [-2,2] requires b≥0 and b≤4; for 0≤b≤4 the quadratic is nonnegative throughout. Its zeros, if any, are isolated, so f is strictly increasing.

working:
$f'(x)=e^xq(x),\quad q(x)=x^2+(a+2)x+(a+2)$. $q(-2)=2-a\ge0,\quad q(2)=3a+10\ge0$ imply $-\dfrac{10}{3}\le a\le2$, where the vertex lies in $[-2,2]$. $q_{\min}=a+2-\dfrac{(a+2)^2}{4}\ge0\iff -2\le a\le2$. Thus $f'\ge0$, with at most isolated zeros, so $f$ is strictly increasing.

Independent check: Let b=a+2. Then f'(x)=e^x(x^2+bx+b). Nonnegativity on [-2,2] requires b≥0 and b≤4; for 0≤b≤4 the quadratic is nonnegative throughout. Its zeros, if any, are isolated, so f is strictly increasing.
solution:
$f'(x)=e^xq(x)$, where $q(x)=x^2+(a+2)x+(a+2)$. Since $e^x>0$, it suffices that $q(x)\ge0$ on $[-2,2]$; its minimum there is nonnegative exactly when $0\le a+2\le4$.
Thus $-2\le a\le2$. The derivative can vanish only at isolated points, so $f$ is strictly increasing throughout this interval.
